construction.shape: Narrow what "brand-new" covers, then bound what is left. Two of three arrival paths carry an anchor from outside the service; the third asks, with a nonce.

paths.enrollment: The head arrives through the person. Row 11’s transcript binds the epoch head, so the five typed symbols authenticate where the lineage is as well as whose key it is. No service trust at all.
paths.migration: A user-held package or fidelity archive carries a signed head (rows 10, §9.3, §14). Same in kind as enrollment: the anchor came from outside the service.
paths.recovery: No surviving device. The only genuinely brand-new case, and what the assertion below is for.

construction.assertion: Ed25519( K_auth ; LP("done/head-assert/v1") || LP(workspace_id) || LP(dec epoch) || LP(hex epoch_head) || LP(hex client_nonce) || LP(dec issued_at) )
construction.client_nonce: 32 fresh bytes from the arriving device, per request
construction.issued_at: Seconds. Displayed to the person, never enforced — a recovering device has no trustworthy clock
rules: Refuse an assertion answering a nonce this device did not send.
Record the head at first contact; from then on §13.5’s ancestor rule applies and this row is finished.
Show the person the epoch, its age and the device list it implies, because on the recovery path that display is the only remaining check.
construction.residual: A hostile authorization service can serve a recovering device a stale, self-consistent head at first contact. It cannot also show current content: revocation is atomic with rotation (§7.5), so a hidden revocation is a hidden generation, and a device on the stale generation cannot read anything written after it. The attack degrades to a partition, which is availability rather than integrity.

not_here.primitives: Ed25519 and SHA-256 KATs are row 1’s, in test/vectors/algorithm-suite.json.
not_here.epoch_head: How an epoch head is computed is §13.5’s and row 7’s. This row consumes it as an opaque digest, which is all it is entitled to assume.
not_here.transport: How the request and answer are framed is row 4’s.

authorization.role: K_auth — the authorization signing key that signs epochs (§13.5). Not row 5’s K_accept.

other_service_key.role: Another key the deployment holds. §13.2 forbids one key doing two jobs, and this is that rule as a vector.

bootstrap_signer.role: Committed in the prior RecoverySet and sealed beside R_priv under the content factor. The recovery code yields it; the service never holds it.

new_credential.role: The replacement device's signing credential. Countersigns the bootstrap on install, so the binding names a device that actually holds the key.

vectors.name: current-head
vectors.why: What a recovering device with no surviving device receives, answering the nonce it sent.

vectors.name: same-head-second-device
vectors.why: The same head for a second arriving device. A different nonce means a different signature, which is what makes the first one unreplayable.

vectors.name: ancestor-head
vectors.why: A genuine assertion for the previous epoch. Correctly signed and correctly nonced — refused only by §13.5’s ancestor rule, and only by a device that already has a head.

recovery_bootstrap.why: A certified recipient set is approved by an eligible content-holding client. A total loss with no surviving device would therefore have had nothing able to approve the replacement -- and the validated four-object theorem would have quietly become a five-object one, the fifth being a device that still works. This is what keeps it at four.
recovery_bootstrap.message: Bootstrap = LP("done/recovery-bootstrap/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(dec observed_epoch) || LP(hex observed_head_digest) || LP(hex service_nonce) || LP(hex prior_recovery_state_digest) || LP(hex recovered_root) || LP(new_credential_id) || LP(hex new_wrapping_key) || LP(hex new_recovery_state_digest) || LP(hex conflict_parent)
recovery_bootstrap.signed_by: the bootstrap signer, committed in the prior RecoverySet and sealed beside R_priv under the same content factor -- so the recovery code yields it and the service never holds it
recovery_bootstrap.countersigned_by: the new credential, which is what proves the named device holds the key it is being bound to

four_objects.account_access: account recovery — the person signs in
four_objects.authorization: the service admits a replacement credential
four_objects.content_key_access: the saved recovery code opens R_priv and, beside it, the bootstrap signer
four_objects.ciphertext: a hosted copy, a surviving replica, or a fidelity archive

recovery_bootstrap.no_fifth_object: The signer is inside the factor-protected recovery object, so possession of the code yields both it and R_priv. Nothing new is independently held.
recovery_bootstrap.freshness: observed_epoch, observed_head_digest and service_nonce carry row 9's bound unchanged: a hostile service can withhold, not forge. conflict_parent lets it serialise competing bootstraps without choosing the winner's contents.
recovery_bootstrap.expected: binds the replacement credential and its wrapping key, from four objects and no surviving client

must_fail.name: replayed-under-another-nonce
must_fail.mutate: The assertion a first device received, offered to a second device that sent its own nonce. **This is the row’s reason to exist**: without the nonce a captured assertion is a standing artifact any relay may re-serve forever, and replay stops requiring the authorization key.

must_fail.name: aad-only-nonce-rewritten-to-match
must_fail.mutate: The captured assertion with its carried nonce **rewritten** to the second device’s, so the device’s own comparison passes and only the signature can refuse it. `replayed-under-another-nonce` above tests the client rule and does not test this: it fails on a string comparison whether or not the nonce is signed at all. The coverage audit found that gap on the one field this row exists for.

must_fail.name: aad-only-stale-head
must_fail.mutate: A current epoch number paired with the previous epoch’s head. Isolates `epoch_head`, and is the attack the whole row is bounding — a self-consistent past served to a device with no history.

must_fail.name: aad-only-wrong-epoch
must_fail.mutate: The current head paired with a different epoch number. Both are bound although the head commits to the number, so neither can be moved against the other.

must_fail.name: aad-only-wrong-workspace
must_fail.mutate: Verify the assertion against another workspace. A device may hold several (§6.1), so this is an ordinary confusion rather than an exotic one.

must_fail.name: aad-only-altered-issued-at
must_fail.mutate: Change the timestamp the device displays. It is not enforced — a recovering device has no trustworthy clock — but it is shown to a person, so it is signed.

must_fail.name: aad-only-renumbered-label
must_fail.mutate: Verify under "done/head-assert/v2". The label is where this carrier authenticates its own version (row 1).

must_fail.name: signed-by-another-service-key
must_fail.mutate: A well-formed assertion signed with a different key the deployment holds. §13.2 forbids one key doing two jobs; row 5’s acceptance key in particular is hot and this one need not be.

must_fail.name: ancestor-offered-after-first-contact
must_fail.mutate: A correctly signed, correctly nonced assertion for epoch 8, offered to a device that has already recorded epoch 9. **The exposure is first contact only** — §13.5’s ancestor rule takes over the moment a head is recorded, and this is that boundary as a vector rather than a sentence.

must_fail.name: bootstrap-signed-by-the-service
must_fail.why: The whole separation, as one signature. The bootstrap signer is committed in the prior RecoverySet and sealed beside R_priv, so a service that can admit a credential still cannot authorize one to receive content. Signed here by another key the deployment holds.

must_fail.name: bootstrap-countersigned-by-another-credential
must_fail.why: The countersignature names the device that actually holds the new wrapping key. Without it the recovering client could bind a credential it does not control, which is the same delayed-delivery shape one actor along.

must_fail.name: bootstrap-with-a-stale-observed-head
must_fail.why: Row 9's bound, at this carrier: a service that withholds cannot forge, but it can offer an older head. Binding the observed head means a bootstrap built against a stale view does not verify against the current one.

must_fail.name: bootstrap-replayed-under-another-nonce
must_fail.why: The service-issued nonce is retired on use. Replaying an otherwise honest bootstrap under a second nonce is how a withheld transition would be re-presented later.

must_fail.name: bootstrap-naming-another-prior-recovery-state
must_fail.why: It must chain from the recovery state the code actually opened. Unbound, a bootstrap could claim succession from a set the recovering party never held.

must_fail.name: bootstrap-substituting-the-new-wrapping-key
must_fail.why: The point of the object. If the key the new credential will receive content on is not bound, the service supplies its own and the recovery hands it the workspace.

must_fail.name: bootstrap-forked-from-another-parent
must_fail.why: Two bootstraps under different conflict parents are two different transitions. The service serialises them; it does not get to choose the winner's contents, and a fork is detectable rather than silent.

must_fail.name: aad-only-bootstrap-service-nonce
must_fail.why: Row 14 §9's move, at this carrier. `bootstrap-replayed-under-another-nonce` above fails on the comparison between the nonce in the object and the one this recovery received -- and that comparison would refuse it just as readily if the nonce were signed by nobody. So this one carries the nonce the verifier is expecting, which forces the refusal onto the signature and is also what a real attacker would present, since those bytes are theirs to edit.

must_fail.name: aad-only-bootstrap-label
must_fail.why: The label doing its own job.

must_fail.name: aad-only-bootstrap-workspace-id
must_fail.why: The bootstrap moved to another workspace.

must_fail.name: aad-only-bootstrap-lineage-id
must_fail.why: The bootstrap moved to another lineage.

must_fail.name: aad-only-bootstrap-observed-epoch
must_fail.why: The epoch the head was observed at.

must_fail.name: aad-only-bootstrap-recovered-root
must_fail.why: The content root the recovery actually opened, which is what a later package verifies against.

must_fail.name: aad-only-bootstrap-new-credential-id
must_fail.why: The credential the binding names, held apart from the key it receives on.

must_fail.name: aad-only-bootstrap-new-recovery-state-digest
must_fail.why: The recovery state the replacement installs, so a bootstrap cannot leave a substituted recipient behind it.
